reason: The dominant variable between conformers is not the fixed aziridine ring but the orientation of the N-substituent chain and the CH2OH group. I first checked the O-H...N contact: a useful intramolecular hydrogen bond requires O-N around 2.7-3.0 Å and H-N under roughly 2.4 Å, with the OH hydrogen pointing at least approximately toward N. Conformers 8, 30, 23, 5, 12, and 27 combine a reasonably short H...N contact with an anti C2-C3-C4-N arrangement; 8 and 30 are additionally anti around C3-C4-C8-O, which avoids gauche C-C/O penalties while still keeping the OH near N. 23, 5, and 12 are close behind because the H-bond is retained but the C3-C4-C8-O unit is gauche; 27 is slightly lower because its H-bond is longer. Conformers 19, 17, 20, and 22 have strong or moderate H-bond contacts but pay extra gauche-butane-type strain in the C2-C3-C4-N and C3-C4-C8-O torsions; among them 19 has the shortest H...N contact. 15, 4, 21, and 13 follow with progressively longer/bent H...N contacts and less ideal chain torsions. The remaining conformers either have O-H pointing away from N (no real hydrogen bond) or have the chain folded with no compensating H-bond; these are less stable. I placed the no-H-bond folded conformers above the open/no-contact set, since the O/N dipole proximity is still mildly favorable. The uncertainty is mainly in the middle and bottom tiers because the differences are small and the files contain no energies.

The molecule contains an amine N-H donor, a primary amide N-H2 donor, a carbonyl O acceptor, and a nitrile N acceptor. I evaluated explicit H...acceptor distances and donor-H...acceptor angles. Intramolecular H-bonds dominate: amide N-H to amine N (H12...N3) is generally stronger than amine N-H to carbonyl O (H4...O10) because the amide N-H is much more acidic and the amine N is a better base. Conformers 25, 26, 27, and 9 have the best amide-NH...amine H-bonds (H...N ~2.11-2.12 Å, angle ~109°). Conformers 11, 12, 28 are next (H...N 2.16-2.18 Å). The best carbonyl H-bonds are in 5 and 19 (H...O 2.15-2.17 Å, angle ~114°), followed by 30, 22, 10 (2.19-2.22 Å, ~110°). Moderate H-bonds are seen in 3, 20, 16, then 8, 4, 1, then 29, 18, 21. Conformers with weak or distorted H-bonds (2, 17, 24, 23, 15) are less stable, and those with no significant H-bond, 13, 14, 6, 7, are least stable. The ordering within closely spaced groups is uncertain because distances/angles differ by only a few hundredths of an angstrom, but the overall ranking reflects best H-bond quality first and absence of H-bonding last.

The molecule is ethyl 2-amino-2-methylacetate (ethyl alaninate). Main stabilizing differences come from intramolecular N-H···O=C vs N-H···O-ester hydrogen bonding, plus weaker steric/rotameric effects. Conformers with N-H pointing toward the carbonyl oxygen and a short N-H···O distance (≈2.35-2.6 Å) are generally the most stable because the carbonyl O is the better acceptor. These are 1, 7, 8, 14, 15, 16; they all show nearly equivalent N-H···O=C contacts, so their relative order is uncertain. Next come conformers with somewhat longer or less linear N-H···O=C contacts (5, 18, 29, 11). Then come conformers stabilized instead by weaker N-H···O-ester hydrogen bonds, with close H···O-ester distances (2.3-2.5 Å) but poorer acceptor strength: 6, 10, 24, 26, 27, 22, 20, 21, 12, 9, 3, 17, 13, 4, 19, 23, 25, 30. The least stable are 2 and 28, where N and carbonyl O are close but both N-H hydrogens point away from the oxygen, so no hydrogen-bond network forms and the arrangement is electrostatically unfavorable. Because many conformers within each group differ only by very small angular/distance changes, the finer ordering is uncertain.

The main stabilizing factor is the intramolecular O-H···O(ether) hydrogen bond between the alcohol OH and the ether oxygen. I estimated the H···O distance and the O-H···O angle from the coordinates. Conformers 12, 5, and 13 have the strongest such contacts (H···O ≈ 2.2 Å, angle ≈ 116°) and are placed at the top. Conformers 30 and 16 have slightly weaker/longer H-bonding angles, followed by 18, 29, 17, 28 with moderate H-bond geometry. Conformers 21, 24, 27, and 9 show only weak H-bonding and have a gauche O···CH3 relationship, so they are ranked next. The remaining conformers lack a productive O-H···O hydrogen bond. Among these, 6, 11, 15, and 25 keep an anti relationship between the ether oxygen and the terminal methyl and are somewhat preferred over the fully extended trans O-C-C-O conformers 1, 2, 8, 10, 14, 19, 20, 23, and 26. The least stable are conformers 4, 3, 7, and 22: 4 has no H-bond and a gauche O···CH3 contact, while 3, 7, and 22 place the O-H away from the ether oxygen with close O···O gauche repulsion. The ordering within similar groups is uncertain because energy differences are small and mostly electrostatic/dispersive.

The molecule is a cyclopropane-diol with a propan-2-yl substituent. The dominant conformational factor is intramolecular O-H...O hydrogen bonding between the two alcohol groups. I evaluated O...O distances and the directionality of each O-H donor toward the other oxygen; shorter distances and more linear O-H...O angles were ranked as more stabilizing. I also inspected steric clashes, especially close contacts between the isopropyl methyl carbons and the OH oxygens or cyclopropane carbons, and avoided over-weighting conformers with severe nonbonded repulsion. Conformer 2 has the shortest, best-aligned intramolecular H-bond (O...O ~2.66 Å, near-linear donor H), making it the most stable. Conformers 1 and 11 have strong H-bonds as well but slightly more steric crowding. The middle group, including 17, 15, 26, 14, 24, 9, 21, 27, and 29, retains meaningful H-bonding but with longer O...O contacts and/or poorer angles. Conformers 13, 10, 3, and 19 have weaker or poorly oriented H-bonding. The remaining conformers lack a good intramolecular H-bond and are generally less stable; among them, 18 and 7 have the fewest close contacts, while the later entries show increasing methyl-OH or methyl-cyclopropane steric clashes. The exact ordering of the middle and lower portions is somewhat uncertain because differences are small, but the division between H-bonded and non-H-bonded structures is clear.

All conformers share the same aziridine-ring scaffold and have no conventional hydrogen-bond donors, so the ranking is dominated by nonbonded steric contacts and side-chain torsional strain. I compared heavy-atom distances between the ethyl methyl group, the methoxymethyl side chain, and the aziridine ring carbons. Conformer 6 has the most splayed arrangement and only mild contacts (roughly 3.08-3.33 Å). Conformers 7 and 4 are also relatively open but have a somewhat shorter C8-C13 contact and additional 3.2-3.3 Å contacts. Conformers such as 10, 16, 22, 23, and 26 are more folded, with several contacts near 3.1-3.2 Å. The least stable conformers have very short O-C contacts below about 3.0 Å, especially 17 and 28 with C-O contacts near 2.87 Å, followed by 19, 2, 30, 11, 14, 21, 13, and 8. The middle ordering is uncertain because the energetic differences are small and H-H contacts are not fully captured by simple heavy-atom distances.

The molecule is 3-methylhexane-1,4-diol with two OH groups, so the dominant stabilizing feature is intramolecular O-H...O hydrogen bonding. I estimated O...O and H...O distances and O-H...O angles from the coordinates. Conformers with short, directional H-bonds (O...O 2.7-2.9 Å, H...O 1.8-1.9 Å, angles near 150-160°) were placed highest. Among these, I ordered by H-bond quality and by counting gauche 1,4 heavy-atom contacts (C...C/C...O <3.4 Å) plus any 1,5 methyl-methyl contacts. Conformer 12 has an excellent H-bond and relatively few severe close contacts; 8, 7, 10, 23, 17, 15, and 19 follow with slightly more strain or slightly less ideal H-bond angles. Conformer 25 has a low gauche count but only a weak, bent H-bond, so it sits near the boundary of the strong-H-bond cluster. Conformers 24, 1, 13, 18, 27, 22, and 30 have good H-bonds but more gauche interactions, while 9 is the most strained of the strongly H-bonded set because of many 1,4 close contacts. Conformers 16 and 3 add a 1,5 methyl-methyl contact to their strong H-bond. Conformers 5 and 28 have weak/bent H-bonds with moderate strain; 20, 21, and 26 are extended non-H-bonded conformers with relatively few gauche contacts. Conformer 6 has a weak bent H-bond and one extra gauche contact. The non-H-bonded extended/strained set (2, 11, 14, 4, 29) is lowest, with 2 and 11 somewhat less strained than 14/4/29. The middle and lower portions of the ranking are uncertain because no energies are provided and several conformers are close in the balance of H-bonding and steric strain.

The molecule is a cyclopropane bearing two hydroxyls (on C4 and C6) and a pendant ketone side chain. I evaluated each conformer primarily for intramolecular O–H···O=C hydrogen bonds, using donor H to carbonyl O distances and approximate O–H···O angles. The strongest hydrogen bonds have H···O distances near 1.88–2.15 Å; these appear in conformers 3, 9, 21, 12, 10, 22, 24, 18, 20, 25, and 7. Among these, the ones with the shortest, most linear H-bonds (3, 9, 21, 12, 10) were ranked highest, while 7 has a longer/less ideal H-bond. The next group (14, 4, 27, 17, 30, 23, 11, 26) shows longer H···O contacts (2.3–2.9 Å) or poor angles, providing weaker stabilization. The remaining conformers lack a significant intramolecular H-bond; their ranking is based on avoided eclipsing interactions and fewer close nonbonded contacts. The ranking is approximate because several conformers are close in energy and subtle steric differences are difficult to quantify without electronic structure calculations.

All conformers share the same C6H10O3 skeleton: CH3-CH(OH)-CH(CHO)-COCH3. The dominant stabilizing feature is an intramolecular O-H···O=C hydrogen bond from the hydroxyl oxygen to either the aldehyde carbonyl oxygen (O9) or the ketone carbonyl oxygen (O12), forming a favorable six-membered hydrogen-bonded ring. From the coordinates I estimated H···O distances and O-H···O angles; conformers with short, well-directed H-bonds are clearly more stable: 19 (1.92 Å, ~138°), 8 (2.01 Å, ~133° plus a weak C-H···O contact), 14 (2.01 Å, ~130°), 17 (2.05 Å, ~131°), 24 (2.11 Å, ~125°), 12 (2.18 Å, ~131°), 2 (2.16 Å, ~123°), 18 (2.18 Å, ~125° with a mild C-H···O contact), 28 (2.19 Å, ~124°), 11 (2.24 Å, ~129°), 3 (2.23 Å, ~124°), and 23 (2.24 Å, ~124°). Conformers lacking that O-H···O H-bond are placed next, with more extended geometries and larger carbonyl O···O separations favored over compact ones with short O···O or C-H···O contacts. The ordering among the non-hydrogen-bonded conformers is the most uncertain because their energy differences are small and arise mainly from weak dispersion, dipole orientation, and subtle steric contacts.

The molecule is a planar 2,5-disubstituted pyrrole bearing an ethyl group and a hydroxymethyl group, so ring strain is not a major differentiator. No conventional intramolecular O-H...N or N-H...O hydrogen bond is present: although some conformers have short N...O or H...O contacts, the donor-hydrogen...acceptor angles are poor (~80-96°), so those contacts are better treated as steric/electrostatic clashes rather than stabilizing H-bonds. The main ranking criteria are therefore close nonbonded contacts between the ethyl methyl carbon and the pyrrole nitrogen, and between the hydroxymethyl oxygen and the pyrrole N-H region. Conformer 10 is clearly the least stable: its methyl carbon approaches the pyrrole nitrogen at only 2.87 Å and a methyl hydrogen comes within 2.60 Å of the N-H hydrogen, a severe steric clash. Conformers 23 and 27 are also strongly destabilized by very short N...O distances (~2.70 Å) and H(N)...O distances (~2.41 Å) with poor H-bond geometry. Conformers 3, 21, and 25 have moderately short N...O contacts (~3.0 Å) combined with the methyl group close to nitrogen, making them less stable. The most stable conformers are the extended anti/anti-type arrangements in which the ethyl methyl and the hydroxymethyl oxygen are both held away from the pyrrole N-H and from each other, especially 1, 14, 11, and 16. Intermediate groups differ by whether the methyl or oxygen is closer to the N-H region; these differences are subtle, so ordering inside those groups is less certain.

The molecule is a flexible hydroxy-aldehyde-alkyne (3-hydroxy-3-methyl-5-hexynal type). The dominant stabilizing factor is intramolecular O-H···O=C hydrogen bonding. Conformers 30, 2, 9, 26, 4, and 18 place the hydroxyl hydrogen close to the aldehyde carbonyl oxygen (H···O distances roughly 1.94–2.14 Å, O···O distances 2.76–2.85 Å) with reasonable O-H···O angles, so these are placed at the top. Among these, 30 has the shortest H···O contact and an anti alkyne arm; 2 and 9 have strong, nearly linear H-bonds; 26 is linear but has a gauche methyl-alkyne orientation; 4 and 18 are more bent/gauche. The next group consists of conformers without O-H···O but with clear O-H···π(alkyne) contacts, e.g. 19, 29, 11, 7, and 8 have H(oxygen) near the C≡C carbons (2.36–2.93 Å), often reinforced by weak C-H···O contacts to the hydroxyl or carbonyl oxygen and an anti rather than gauche alkyne arm. These are more stable than conformers lacking any strong donor contact. The middle/uncertain region involves weaker O-H···π, C-H···O contacts, and gauche methyl-alkyne strain: 15, 14, 3, 21, 5, 17, 6, and 23 are ordered by how close the O-H is to the alkyne and whether extra aldehyde/methylene C-H···O contacts compensate for the gauche strain. Conformers 22, 24, and 27 are anti but have only weak C-H···O contacts, so they rank below the O-H···π set. Conformers 13, 16, and 28 retain an aldehyde C-H···O contact but are gauche and lack strong O-H interactions. The least stable are 25, 12, 1, 20, and 10, which lack strong directional hydrogen bonds and show increasing methyl-alkyne gauche/eclipsing strain; 10 appears the most crowded with the shortest methyl-alkyne contact and no compensating interaction. The exact order in the middle is somewhat uncertain, but the extremes are clear.

The ring is a tetrahydrofuran bearing a methyl at C2 and a 2-hydroxyethyl sidechain at C6. The dominant intramolecular stabilization is an O-H···O(ring-ether) hydrogen bond. Using O5 as the ring ether oxygen, O9 as the hydroxyl oxygen, and the hydroxyl H, I identified strong H-bonds in conformers 8, 11, 24, 26, 28, and 29: O5···O9 distances are ~2.8 Å and O5···HO distances are ~2.0 Å with O-H···O angles near 130–140°. Among these, 29, 11, 24, and 26 have the best H-bond geometry; 8 has a slightly less linear angle, and 28 has a longer/weaker H-bond and an additional close methyl–OH contact. Conformer 18 has only a weak/long H-bond (O5···HO ≈ 2.6 Å, poor angle), so it ranks after the strongly H-bonded set. The remaining conformers lack intramolecular H-bonds. I then penalized folded sidechains that place the terminal CH2/OH close to the methyl group; the worst contacts occur in 9, 10, 20, 21, and 22. Extended sidechains with no severe methyl–sidechain clashes occupy the middle ranks. Differences among the middle/lower non-H-bonded conformers are subtle and therefore the exact ordering there is somewhat uncertain.

All conformers have the same covalent connectivity; the energetic differences are conformational. The possible intramolecular hydrogen-bond donors are the imine N-H and the aldehyde C-H, while the aldehyde carbonyl O and the ether O can act as acceptors. I inspected the nonbonded N-H...O=C, C-H...O, C-H...N, O...O, and key C-C/O torsional relationships from the coordinates. No perfectly linear intramolecular hydrogen bond is present, but conformers 30 and 20 show the closest N-H...O=C contacts (~2.8 Å) together with very short aldehyde C-H...N contacts (~2.35 Å), so they appear most stabilized. Conformers 29 and 6 also have very short C-H...N contacts but the N-H vector is less well oriented toward the carbonyl oxygen. Conformers 21, 3, 27, 1, and 2 combine an anti arrangement around the central C-C bond with moderate C-H...O/N contacts. Conformers 19, 16, and 4 have good C-H...O(ether) distances but the angles are bent, so they are mid-ranking. More extended conformers such as 15, 14, 24, 28, 22, 12, and 8 avoid severe steric strain but lack comparable intramolecular donor-acceptor contacts, so they sit lower. The least stable group consists of conformers with closer repulsive O...O contacts or several unfavorable gauche/non-interacting arrangements, e.g. 5, 10, 13, 25, and 23. The ordering is approximate because several interactions are weak and bent, so the differences among many adjacent entries are subtle.

The molecule is a cyclohexene ring with a C=C double bond, an allylic methyl substituent, and a homoallylic CH2OH side chain. The main stability factors are ring puckering, 1,3-diaxial-type repulsion between the methyl and CH2OH groups, close H...H contacts, and possible O-H...pi hydrogen bonding from the hydroxyl H to the C=C bond. I estimated OH...pi contacts by comparing the position of the hydroxyl H with the two alkene carbons: conformers 2, 8, 9, 12, 29, and 30 have H-to-alkene distances near 2.3-2.9 A, suggesting favorable OH...pi interactions. Conformers 29, 8, and 30 combine this OH...pi contact with a long methyl-to-CH2OH separation, so they are the most stable. Conformer 2 also has a good OH...pi contact with only modest methyl/side-chain proximity. Conformers 12 and 9 have strong OH...pi geometry but shorter methyl-to-CH2OH distances, indicating some 1,3-type diaxial crowding; they are still likely stabilized by the H-bond and C-H...O contacts. Most remaining conformers have no OH...pi contact and have substituents in equatorial-like or opposite arrangements; they are moderately stable, with subtle differences in side-chain orientation. Conformer 11 is diaxial-like without compensating H-bonding. Conformers 4, 6, 7, 10, 15, 20, and 22 show short nonbonded H...H contacts below about 2.4 A, making them the least stable; among them, 7 has the shortest severe contact, followed by 4 and 15, then the doubles-contact set 6/20/22, and 10 has the least severe single contact. Overall ranking is most reliable at the extremes; the middle group is uncertain because nonbonded differences are small.

The molecule is an N-formyl amino alcohol: a flexible formamide connected to a branched 3-hydroxy-2-methylpropyl chain. The main stabilizing interactions are intramolecular hydrogen bonds and the main destabilizing factors are steric 1,4-type clashes and poor backbone torsions. Conformers 16, 20, 1, 9, 13, 3, 2, 15, 11, and 10 place the hydroxyl O-H close to the amide carbonyl oxygen, giving an O-H···O=C hydrogen bond; those with the more linear and shorter O-H···O contacts and anti C1···C7 arrangements rank highest. In this group, 16 and 20 have nearly linear H-bonds; 1 and 9 combine strong H-bonds with an anti backbone; 13 has a very short H···O contact but a slightly less ideal angle; 3 has a good H-bond but a close C1···C7 gauche contact, so it is placed a little lower. The next most stable set, 18, 6, 19, 28, 14, 8, and 7, has the amide N-H donating to the alcohol oxygen (N-H···O-H); among these, 18, 6, and 19 have the best distances/angles, while 8 and 7 are more bent. Conformer 22 has only a weak, bent N-H···O alcohol contact. The remaining conformers lack a strong intramolecular H-bond: 25 and 26 are extended anti conformers with no severe clashes, 4 is also reasonably extended, and 29/30/12 follow. The final group has close C1···C7 contacts and no compensating H-bond, with 17, 23, 24, 27, 21, and 5 being the least stable. The largest uncertainties are within clusters of similar H-bond geometries, especially 3 vs 13 and 22/25/26/4.

The molecule is an aziridine-containing 1,3-diol. I treated the fixed aziridine ring as a rigid unit and compared conformers mainly by intramolecular hydrogen-bonding and by close O···N contacts that are not stabilized by a proper O–H···N bond. The strongest stabilizing interactions are O–H···N hydrogen bonds: conformer 1 has O1–H···N with H···N ≈ 2.13 Å and a nearly linear angle, so it is placed first; conformer 23 has a similar but longer/bent O–H···N contact (H···N ≈ 2.32 Å) and is second. Next comes a cluster of good O–H···O hydrogen bonds. Conformer 16 has a very good O–H···O geometry (H···O ≈ 1.96 Å, angle ≈ 147°) without a close O···N repulsion, so it leads this group. Conformers 30, 5, 20, and 22 have short O–H···O distances; 30 has an especially short H···O contact but also a close O···N contact, adding some uncertainty. Conformers 9, 29, 26, 7, 12, 3, 8, 11, 14, 4, and 13 form a continuous series of stronger to weaker O–H···O hydrogen bonds, with variations in H···O distance and O–H···O angle. Conformers 24, 28, and 21 have only poor-angle or longer H-bonding contacts and are less stabilized. The remaining conformers lack a strong intramolecular O–H···O or O–H···N hydrogen bond; among these, 18 and 2 have weak bent N–H···O or O–H···N contacts and are slightly higher in stability, while 6, 10, 15, 27, 17, 19, and 25 have few or no compensating stabilizing contacts. Conformer 25 was placed last because it shows no significant intramolecular H-bond and no compensating favorable electrostatic contact. The middle ordering, especially within the O–H···O cluster and among the weakly interacting conformers, is uncertain because the energy differences are subtle.

The molecule is an acyclic N-H imidate ester with a terminal OH: CH3-C(=NH)-O-(CH2)4-OH. The main stability differences come from intramolecular hydrogen bonding between the terminal O-H/N-H and the imidate O or imine N. A constant close N-H...O5 contact (~2.6 Å) appears in most conformers and was treated as a background interaction, not the main discriminator. The terminal O-H...O5 hydrogen bond is the strongest and most consistent stabilizing feature. Conformers 18, 27, 22, and 29 have short, well-oriented O-H...O5 contacts (roughly 1.9-2.0 Å and near-linear to ~150°), so they rank highest. Conformer 18 has the shortest and most linear O-H...O5 interaction. Conformer 6 is next because it forms a reciprocal, albeit longer and more bent, O-H...N plus N-H...O10 pair. Conformers 3 and 4 have genuine but less linear/longer O-H...O5 H-bonds. Conformers 24, 16, 13, and 10 have only weak/long or poorly oriented donor-acceptor contacts. The remaining conformers lack strong intramolecular H-bonds; their ordering is governed mostly by chain torsion and folding, and I ordered the more extended anti-like chains ahead of shorter folded chains without compensating H-bonds. The tail ordering, especially among 28, 8, and 12, is the most uncertain because the differences are small.

The molecule is a nitrile-ether-cyclopropane chain: N≡C-CH2-O-CH2-CH2-cyclopropyl. There are no hydrogen-bond donors, so the ranking is governed by conformational strain: anti vs gauche preferences around the C–C and C–O bonds, and close nonbonded contacts between the ether oxygen and the cyclopropane ring. I used the coordinates to estimate key 1,4 distances: C2···C5 for the C2–C3–O–C5 torsion, C3···C6 for the C3–O–C5–C6 torsion, and O···C7 for the O–C5–C6–C7 torsion. Conformers with all three torsions anti place the nitrile, ether oxygen, and cyclopropyl group farthest apart and were ranked highest. Conformers with an O···C7 contact below about 3.0 Å have a noticeable O/cyclopropane clash and were ranked lower. Intermediate C2···C5 or C3···C6 distances around 3.1–3.4 Å were treated as skew/strained and penalized less than full gauche but more than anti. The main uncertainty is the rotation of the cyclopropane ring about C6–C7, since C8 and C9 are nearly equivalent and a close contact to one ring CH2 often accompanies a larger distance to the other; I treated ring-rotation differences as minor unless a very short C5···C8/C9 or O···C7 contact was present.

The common framework is a 7-membered cyclic ether with one endocyclic C=C and an exocyclic CH2OH group. I used the coordinates to check the strongest expected stabilizing interaction, O-H···O(ether), by looking at the hydroxyl H to ring-ether O distance. Only conformers 8 and 7 place that H close enough (roughly 2.9 Å) with a plausible O-H···O angle; all other conformers either have the OH pointing away or have H···O > 3.3 Å. Therefore 8 and 7 are placed highest, with 8 slightly ahead because its H···O distance is marginally shorter and it has fewer additional close OH···H contacts. The remaining conformers lack a real intramolecular H-bond to the ether oxygen. I then checked for severe nonbonded clashes involving the CH2OH group; 12, 20, 25, 4, 9, 30, 28, and 13 show the shortest contacts in the 2.2-2.5 Å range, so they are placed lowest. Most of the middle conformers are sterically less distinctive, and their ordering is uncertain; I ranked them using progressively shorter closest contacts and more folded O1···O11 arrangements as rough proxies for increasing strain.

All conformers share the same fused oxetane/cyclobutane scaffold, so the largest single stabilizing difference is intramolecular O-H···O(ether) hydrogen bonding. Conformer 14 has the best H-bond geometry: hydroxyl H···O_ether ≈ 2.00 Å with a nearly linear O-H···O angle (~164°). Conformer 9 is also clearly H-bonded (H···O ≈ 2.06 Å, angle ≈ 153°) and is placed second. Every other conformer has the hydroxyl hydrogen pointing away from the ring ether oxygen, so their ranking is governed by side-chain torsion and steric contacts. Conformers with an anti O-C-C-C side-chain arrangement (O1···C5 distances near 3.7–3.8 Å) are generally less crowded and rank next; among these, 5, 16 and 17 have the least additional 1,4 C···C/O···C crowding. Then come other anti-like conformers with closer C3···C15 contacts, followed by intermediate/twisted side-chain conformers. Finally, the most folded/gauche conformers place the hydroxyl group near ring carbons or show short nonbonded contacts (C3···C15 < ~3.1 Å, O1···C15/C7 ≈ 3.0–3.2 Å, or O1···O_ether contacts without H-bond directionality) and are ranked lower. The exact ordering within the middle and lower groups is uncertain because these are subtle steric differences, but the H-bonded conformers are clear outliers at the top.

The molecule is a cis-1,2-disubstituted cyclobutane: a cyclobutane ring bearing a CH2CH2OH side chain at one carbon and an OH at the adjacent ring carbon. The main stability factors are (1) intramolecular O-H...O hydrogen bonding, (2) gauche/anti conformations along the side-chain O-C-C-C and C-C-C-C chains, (3) close nonbonded H...H contacts, and (4) ring puckering. All rings are nearly planar (small dihedral angles), so ring-strain differences are minor and are not the deciding factor. Conformers 3, 4, 8, and 14 have O...O distances of 2.87-2.92 Å with near-linear O-H...O hydrogen bonds; these are distinctly the most stable. Among them, 3 has the shortest H...O distance (1.91 Å) and most linear H-bond (169°) with only a mild side-chain-ring H...H contact; 14 has a strong H-bond (1.94 Å, 163°) and no significant clash; 4 has a slightly weaker H-bond (1.99 Å, 160°) but is clean; 8 has a strong H-bond (1.92 Å, 170°) but a clear transannular H...H clash of 2.14 Å that destabilizes it. After the H-bonded group, the best non-H-bonded conformer is 11, which is fully anti along both side-chain torsions and has no close contacts. The next set has exactly one gauche interaction: 15, 1, 10, 28, and 18 have O-C-C-C gauche but C-C-C-C anti, while 24, 6, 30, 12, 22, and 27 have O-C-C-C anti but C-C-C-C gauche. These two sub-blocks are of similar energy; the O...C gauche is slightly less costly than the C...C gauche, so the former are placed a little higher. All of these lack severe transannular clashes. The remaining conformers have two gauche interactions; 7, 9, 13, 16, 19, 25, and 26 have near-ideal gauche torsions and no clashes, so they rank next. Conformers 17, 2, 20, and 21 have somewhat less ideal (larger) gauche angles but no severe contacts. Conformer 29 has close O...O without a hydrogen bond, a near-eclipsed C-C-C-C torsion, and no compensating H-bond, making it worse. Conformers 5 and 23 combine two gauche interactions with short transannular H...H contacts (2.26 Å and 2.16 Å, respectively); 23 is the worst. The ordering within the middle 1-gauche and 2-gauche blocks is uncertain because the energy differences are small (<0.5 kcal/mol), but the major divisions (H-bonded > anti nonbonded > one-gauche > two-gauche > clashing) are robust.

No genuine intramolecular N-H...O=C hydrogen bond is present in any conformer: every N...O distance is >4.5 Å, so relative stability is controlled by torsional strain and nonbonded clashes. The decisive coordinates are (i) the O...Cγ distance across the O=C-C-C unit and (ii) the Cα...Calkyne distance across the C-C-C-C≡ unit.
